title: Enduring Love
full_review:
Here's a frustrating paradox. From its first moments, "Enduring Love" (Paramount Classics) confidently pulls you into its story, but about midway through, the film shifts gears and becomes a run-of-the-mill thriller, though its complex themes continue to provide texture and resonance.

In the opening scene, Joe Rose (Daniel Craig) and his girlfriend Claire (Samantha Morton) are about to enjoy an idyllic champagne picnic in the English countryside when suddenly they hear cries for help as a red hot-air balloon sweeps by, wildly out of control.

Joe and three other passers-by attempt to tackle the balloon and rescue the little boy inside. At first, they seem to have it under control and nearly grounded, when suddenly everyone lets go, except for one man who drifts high into the sky dangling by a rope, until he finally drops off in exhaustion.

The scene haunts Joe, a university professor, who prides himself on his rational thinking, and he begins to obsess about the incident, scientifically trying to dissect the details, wondering if he dropped off first and, if so, if that caused the others to drop off and thereby caused the man's death.

At the height of this paranoia, he hears from the hermitlike Jed Parry (Rhys Ifans) who had insisted they pray together in the field right after the accident. Jed says he has something to tell him, and they must meet. Joe reluctantly agrees, but Jed never quite articulates the revelation Joe expects. Instead, he keeps referring to the "something (that) has passed between them."

Joe begins to be bothered by Jed showing up at every turn -- alternately fascinated and fearing what Jed might reveal, as Jed seems to know what's going on in his very soul. The obsession with the incident and the increasingly intrusive presence of Jed begins to seriously strain Joe's relationship with Claire.

About midway through, however, the story veers into much less profound territory, as Jed's single-minded persistence turns into rather conventional stalking. (Apparently, in the book, Jed was an outright stalker right from the get-go.) At this point, the film turns into a more routine thriller, almost a male version of "Fatal Attraction," and less about the more fascinating themes of guilt and responsibility, and how one random incident can fatefully change one's life.

The chameleonlike Craig and Ifans are superb as always, so different in each film they do, and completely inhabiting their characters. Craig is all academic rationality until he begins to unhinge; Ifans a sweet loner who subtly projects more and more menace. Morton, though sporting long hair after the gamin cut she's had for her last several films, projects her competent brand of vulnerability.

Roger Michell directs playwright Joe Penhall's free adaptation of Ian McEwan's acclaimed 1998 novel about the "conflicts between love and logic, science and wonder, obsession and redemption," with sensitivity, bringing out the best in his actors. Michell has said the title raises the question of how "one endures being loved," while Penhall, who wrote the screenplay, believes it refers to "unrequited love." Take your pick.

In spite of the intense plot turns that lead to violence, the film ultimately ends on a redemptive note. And though the overall film is flawed, the superb performances and compelling suspense still make "Enduring Love" a worthwhile experience.

Because of adult themes, some implied sexuality, some rough language and violence with associated blood, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
